$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

**(b) Current flux through oriented $3$-faces and chains.** Let $J$ be a
smooth vector field on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **current
$3$-form** of $J$ is the contraction

$$\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g,$$

the interior product of the $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ with $J$
([[def-interior-product-of-a-form-by-a-vector-field]]).

By a **smooth singular $k$-simplex** of $M$ — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-simplex` (differential-geometry track),
restated here so this page is self-contained — we mean a map
$\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ whose domain is the standard $k$-simplex
$$\Delta^k=\Bigl\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:t_i\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_it_i=1\Bigr\},$$
for which there exist an open set $O\subseteq A^k=\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\sum_it_i=1\}$
containing $\Delta^k$ and a smooth map $\bar\sigma:O\to M$ with
$\bar\sigma|_{\Delta^k}=\sigma$; the extension is not part of the simplex
data, and degenerate parametrizations are allowed. With the integration of
forms over such simplices
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]), a **$3$-face** is
a smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$, and the **flux of $J$ through
$\sigma$** is the real number

$$\Phi_J(\sigma):=\int_\sigma\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

A **finite smooth singular $k$-chain** — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes`, restated here —
is a finite formal real linear combination $\Sigma=\sum_i c_i\sigma_i$ of
smooth singular $k$-simplices. For such a $3$-chain the **flux of $J$ through
$\Sigma$** is defined additively,

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma):=\sum_i c_i\,\Phi_J(\sigma_i),$$

a definition independent of the written expression for $\Sigma$, because a
finite formal sum is evaluated by adding the finitely many coefficients and
inserting a zero coefficient changes nothing. $\Phi_J(\Sigma)$ is the **charge**
of the current $J$ assigned to $\Sigma$ when the model reads $J$ as a conserved
current; that reading belongs to the physical postulates and is not part of
this definition.

**(c) Non-null faces and their unit normals.** A $3$-dimensional linear subspace
$H\subseteq T_pM$ is **nondegenerate** for $g_p$ when the restriction of $g_p$
to $H$ is nondegenerate, equivalently when $H\cap H^\perp=\{0\}$ in the
orthogonality of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. A
smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$ is **non-null at** a parameter point $t$
when the span of the three velocity vectors
$\sigma_*\partial_1|_t,\sigma_*\partial_2|_t,\sigma_*\partial_3|_t$ has
dimension $3$ and is nondegenerate at $\sigma(t)$, and **non-null** when this holds at every
parameter point. For a non-null face the **unit normal** $\nu$ at that point is
the unique vector of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$ with $\nu\in H^\perp$,
$g(\nu,\nu)\in\{-1,+1\}$ and $(\nu,\sigma_*\partial_1,\sigma_*\partial_2,
\sigma_*\partial_3)$ a positively oriented basis of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$; its
existence, uniqueness and its sign $\varepsilon:=g(\nu,\nu)$ are proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c), together
with the density identity of clause (c) used to read $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ on
such a face. Rank-deficient faces and rank-three faces with degenerate induced
metric are not assigned a unit normal; their flux is defined
by the $3$-form $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ itself, as in clause (b).

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with an
orientation, metric-selected connection $\nabla$, metric volume form
$\mathrm{vol}_g$ and current flux $\Phi_J$ as in
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]], and let $J$ be a smooth vector
field on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). Write
$\nabla_aJ^a$ for the divergence of $J$.

**(a) Exterior derivative of the current form.** As smooth $4$-forms on $M$,

$$d\bigl(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g\bigr)=\bigl(\nabla_aJ^a\bigr)\mathrm{vol}_g .$$

**(b) Flux balance (Stokes).** For every finite smooth singular $4$-chain $C$
of $M$ — a finite formal real sum of smooth singular $4$-simplices, the
library convention `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes` restated
in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) — and the flux
$\Phi_J$ of the induced boundary $3$-chain
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]],
[[thm-stokes-theorem-for-smooth-singular-chains]]),

$$\Phi_J(\partial C)=\int_C\bigl(\nabla_aJ^a\bigr)\mathrm{vol}_g .$$

Consequently, if $\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$ for smooth singular $3$-chains
$\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2,B$, then

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma_2)-\Phi_J(\Sigma_1)=-\Phi_J(B)+\int_C\bigl(\nabla_aJ^a\bigr)\mathrm{vol}_g .$$

In particular, if $\nabla_aJ^a=0$ on $C$ then
$\Phi_J(\Sigma_2)-\Phi_J(\Sigma_1)=-\Phi_J(B)$, and if moreover
$\Phi_J(B)=0$ then $\Phi_J(\Sigma_2)=\Phi_J(\Sigma_1)$: equal charges need a
vanishing side flux, not merely a divergence-free current.

**(c) Non-null face formula.** Let $\sigma$ be a smooth singular $3$-simplex —
a map $\sigma:\Delta^3\to M$ admitting a smooth extension to a neighbourhood
of the standard $3$-simplex inside its affine plane, the convention restated
in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) — that is
non-null at a parameter point $t$
([[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (c)), with
$v_i:=\sigma_*\partial_i|_t$ spanning the hyperplane $H$ and with the unit
normal $\nu^{*}$ adapted to the ordered basis $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ as in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c); write
$\varepsilon:=g_{\sigma(t)}(\nu^{*},\nu^{*})\in\{-1,1\}$. Then

$$\sigma^{*}\bigl(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g\bigr)(\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3)\big|_{t} =\varepsilon\,g_{\sigma(t)}\bigl(J,\nu^{*}\bigr)\sqrt{\bigl|\det\bigl(g_{\sigma(t)}(v_i,v_j)\bigr)\bigr|} .$$

Equivalently, the tangent vector $J$ is decomposed as
$J=\varepsilon g(J,\nu^{*})\nu^{*}+w'$ with $w'\in H$, and only the normal
component contributes to the flux through the face.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) whose underlying manifold carries an
orientation ([[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]), and let
$w$ and the local forms $\mathrm{vol}_{g,U}$ be as in
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (a).

**(a) Chart independence.** Let $(U,x)$ and $(V,y)$ be oriented charts with
$x=\varphi\circ y$ on the overlap of their domains, where $\varphi$ is the
smooth transition map; write $g_{ab}$ and $g'_{ab}$ for the metric components
in the two charts and $w=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$,
$w'=\sqrt{|\det(g'_{ab})|}$. Then

$$\det(g'_{ab})=\bigl(\det D\varphi\bigr)^{2}\det\bigl(g_{ab}\circ\varphi\bigr),\qquad w'=\bigl(\det D\varphi\bigr)\,(w\circ\varphi),$$

and the local forms agree on the overlap,

$$\varphi^{*}\bigl(w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\bigr)=w'\,dy^0\wedge dy^1\wedge dy^2\wedge dy^3 .$$

Consequently there is a unique smooth nowhere-vanishing $4$-form
$\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — whose restriction to the
domain of every oriented chart $(U,x)$ is $w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge
dx^3$; it is a smooth section with nowhere-zero values and positive on the
given orientation.

**(b) Value on orthonormal frames.** For every $p\in M$ and every positively
oriented ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ with
$g_p(e_A,e_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$,

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1 .$$

**(c) Non-null hyperplanes: normal and density.** Let $p\in M$, let
$H\subseteq T_pM$ be a $3$-dimensional subspace that is nondegenerate for
$g_p$, and let $v_1,v_2,v_3$ be an ordered basis of $H$. Then $H^{\perp}$ is
one-dimensional and nondegenerate and $H=(H^{\perp})^{\perp}$. Let
$u\in H^{\perp}\setminus\{0\}$ and write $\nu:=u/\sqrt{|g_p(u,u)|}$, so that
$\varepsilon:=g_p(\nu,\nu)\in\{-1,1\}$. If $\delta\in\{-1,1\}$ is the sign for
which $(\delta\nu,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ is a positively oriented basis of $T_pM$, then
$\nu^{*}:=\delta\nu$ is the **unit normal to $H$ adapted to the ordered basis**
$(v_1,v_2,v_3)$; it satisfies $g_p(\nu^{*},\nu^{*})=\varepsilon$,
$g_p(\nu^{*},h)=0$ for every $h\in H$, and it is the unique vector with these
two properties for which $(\nu^{*},v_1,v_2,v_3)$ is positively oriented.
Moreover

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(\nu^{*},v_1,v_2,v_3)=\sqrt{\bigl|\det\bigl(g_p(v_i,v_j)\bigr)\bigr|}.$$

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

derivations.claim: (The current is divergence-free.) By [L1], $\nabla_aJ^a=\partial_aJ^a=\partial_1(1)=0$: $J$ satisfies the hypothesis of the refuted statement.

(The adapted normal.) The velocity vectors of $\sigma$ are $v_1=\partial_0$, $v_2=\partial_2$, $v_3=\partial_3$, spanning the hyperplane $H=\{v^1=0\}$, which is nondegenerate (it is the $g$-orthogonal complement of the spacelike vector $\partial_1$). The vector $
u^{*}:=-\partial_1$ lies in $H^{\perp}$, has $g(
u^{*},
u^{*})=1$, and the ordered basis $(-\partial_1,\partial_0,\partial_2,\partial_3)$ has determinant $-\det(\partial_1,\partial_0,\partial_2,\partial_3)=+1$ in the identity chart, so $(
u^{*},v_1,v_2,v_3)$ is positively oriented: $
u^{*}$ is the adapted unit normal.

(The flux.) By [L3] with $\varepsilon=g(
u^{*},
u^{*})=1$, $g(J,
u^{*})=g(\partial_1,-\partial_1)=-1$ and $\det(g(v_i,v_j))=\det\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1)=-1$, so $\sqrt{|\det(g(v_i,v_j))|}=1$ and the pullback $\sigma^*(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g)$ is the constant scalar coefficient $\varepsilon g(J,
u^{*})\cdot1=-1$ times $dt_1\wedge dt_2\wedge dt_3$. By [L2] and [L4], $$\Phi_J(\sigma)=\int_{\Delta^3}(-1)\,dt_1dt_2dt_3=-	frac16
eq0 .$$

(Conclusion.) The field $J=\partial_1$ is divergence-free on $M$, yet its flux through the smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$ is $-1/6$, not zero. Hence the displayed statement is refuted: divergence-freedom is a differential condition on $J$, while the flux through a single face depends on the face and its orientation.

boundaries.reason: An explicit field and affine simplex on four-dimensional space are given; no empty instance arises.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: the divergence vanishes identically, the hypothesis of the refuted statement, while step 2.1 computes a nonzero flux, isolating the failure of the implication.
step 1.2: the adapted normal is the single vector opposite the first coordinate direction with density factor one; step 2.1 obtains the pullback constant from that one pairing.
step 1.2: the hyperplane spanned by the velocity vectors is nondegenerate, being the orthogonal complement of a spacelike coordinate vector; null faces are excluded by the face-formula hypotheses.

step 2.1 integrates a constant over the standard simplex, whose faces are the loci where one parameter vanishes; the constant coefficient makes those parameter-boundary contributions cancel in the integral over the simplex.

boundaries.reason: The field, the simplex and the orientation are explicitly fixed; no selection occurs.
A refutation of one implication is given; no equivalence is asserted.
The converse statement is neither claimed nor used.

risk_review.notes: Read all four steps. J=partial_1 has zero coordinate divergence. Velocities partial_0,partial_2,partial_3 have Gram diag(-1,1,1): this is a timelike face, with spacelike adapted normal -partial_1 and positively oriented ambient tuple. The pullback three-form has scalar coefficient -1; its integral is -1/6, nonzero. Reader title repair is sound; amended the separate incorrect phrase “1-form coefficient” to “scalar coefficient”. Finite simplex volume computation uses iterated polynomial integration on the simplex; orientation reversal changes sign only.

citations.quote:
Adopt one of the two presentations of the framework's field law, that is,
[[post-gr-classical-gravitational-action]] or
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]], for a model with geometric data and matter
sector satisfying [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be the model's smooth
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with metric-selected connection $\nabla$
and curvature tensors $R^{a}{}_{bcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$,
$G_{ab}$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]), let $T$ be the model's smooth
symmetric stress-energy tensor field on the matter domain
([[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]]), let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be the
constant parameter and $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$ as in
[[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $U\subseteq M$ be the
model's open matter domain and suppose the field law holds on $U$,

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}\qquad\text{on }U .$$

**(a) Necessary conservation.** $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$. Consequently a
prescribed smooth symmetric $T$ with $\nabla^aT_{ab}\neq0$ at some point cannot
satisfy the field law there with that proposed metric; the divergence is
computed using its metric-selected connection, and may change if the metric
is changed.

**(b) Trace.** On $U$, $g^{ab}T_{ab}$ satisfies
$-S+4\Lambda=\kappa\,g^{ab}T_{ab}$.

**(c) Parameter variation.** If instead $\Lambda:U\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth
function and the field law $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$ holds on $U$
with that function in place of a constant, then on $U$

$$\kappa\nabla^aT_{ab}=\partial_b\Lambda .$$

Consequently, at every point where $d\Lambda\ne0$, the equation requires
$\nabla^aT_{ab}\ne0$; where $d\Lambda=0$, this identity imposes conservation.
A smooth $\Lambda$ can be locally constant but nonconstant across disconnected
components of $U$, in which case this identity does not force nonconservation.

**(d) A vacuum solution.** In the global vacuum example take
$U=M=\mathbb R^4$ with the identity chart and the flat metric
$g_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ (a smooth Lorentzian metric
with time orientation $N=\partial_0$), the field law with $T=0$ and $\Lambda=0$
holds: $G=0$ and $S=0$ for the flat metric. With $T=0$ and $\Lambda\neq0$ it
fails, since $G+\Lambda g=\Lambda g\neq0$.

**(e) Energy conditions are additional assumptions.** Neither adopted
presentation of the field law contains a clause imposing any of the weak, null,
dominant or strong energy conditions of [[def-gr-energy-conditions]]; none of
the four is a universal consequence of that equation, as the direct-equation
perfect-fluid model in the proof shows. Particular matter models may imply
energy conditions; when not derived, they are additional assumptions in the
sense of clause (iv) of [[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]].

**(f) Perfect-fluid rest-frame reading.** Let $(\varepsilon,p,n)$ be a
perfect-fluid model on its matter domain, with derived tensor
$T=(\varepsilon+p)n^\flat\otimes n^\flat+pg$
([[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]]), and at any $p\in U$ let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be a $g_p$-orthonormal basis with $e_0=n_p$. Then
$T_{AB}=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon,p,p,p)$ in that basis, and at $p$

$$T\ \text{satisfies WEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon\ge0\ \text{and}\ \varepsilon+p\ge0,$$

$$T\ \text{satisfies NEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon+p\ge0,\qquad T\ \text{satisfies DEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon\ge|p|,$$

$$T\ \text{satisfies SEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon+3p\ge0\ \text{and}\ \varepsilon+p\ge0 .$$

In particular a model with $\varepsilon>0$ and $p=-\varepsilon$ satisfies the
NEC, WEC and DEC and violates the SEC; the inequality signs here are those of
the strict-timelike convention of [[def-gr-energy-conditions]], under which
continuity extensions to the causal cone are not assumed.

Adopt as the field law of the direct-equation presentation of the classical
gravitational framework, for models satisfying
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]], the following statement.

**(i) The equation.** Let $(M,g,N)$ be the model's smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold with metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12Sg_{ab}$ be the Einstein tensor of that
connection ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Let
$T$ be the model's stress-energy tensor field on its matter domain
$U\subseteq M$ ([[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]]) and let
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be a constant parameter with dimension
$\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $G_N>0$, $c>0$ the constants of
[[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Adopt

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}\,T_{ab}\qquad\text{on }U$$

as the field law of the model. Writing
$\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$ and $T_{ab}=g_{ac}g_{bd}T^{cd}$ for the lowered tensor,
the equation reads $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$

**(ii) Matter content.** The equation constrains the metric and the matter of
the model jointly. A model specifies its matter sector as in
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]]: a scalar-field model with its action
and stress-energy tensor ([[def-gr-scalar-field-matter-model]]), or a dust or perfect-fluid model with prescribed
stress-energy tensor and matter equations. The consistency condition that
every solution must satisfy, $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$, is not adopted separately; it
is a consequence of the equation and of the contracted second Bianchi identity
and is derived in [[pthm-gr-einstein-consistency-and-energy-conditions]].

**(iii) Alternative presentation.** The action formulation of the same field
law is adopted separately in [[post-gr-classical-gravitational-action]]. A
model adopts exactly one of the two presentations. They are alternative
presentations of one classical field law: the action-to-equation theorem of
this page identifies the equation obtained from stationarity of the total
action with the equation displayed in clause (i), and the direct presentation
is not an additional premise of an action-formulated model.

**(iv) Status and scope.** The equation is an adopted law of the model. It is
not derived from mathematical symmetry, from the equivalence principle, or
from observation; covariance and correspondence arguments motivate but do not
prove it. No numerical value of $c$, $G_N$ or $\Lambda$ is asserted, and no
claim is made that any particular metric or matter configuration solves the
equation or describes nature. The smooth-branch exclusions of
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]] apply: distributional or
lower-dimensional sources, boundaries with junction conditions, and non-smooth
fields are outside this formulation. Comparisons of a model's predictions with
data test the combined model — geometry, matter content and this law — and
agreement is evidence about that combination, not a proof of the postulate.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open matter domain
([[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]]).

**(a) Data.** A **perfect-fluid model** on $U$ is a triple $(\varepsilon,p,n)$
consisting of two smooth functions $\varepsilon,p:U\to\mathbb R$, the **rest
energy density** and the **pressure**, and a smooth future-directed unit
timelike vector field $n$ on $U$ with $g_p(n_p,n_p)=-1$ and
$g_p(n_p,N_p)<0$ at every $p$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). No positivity of
$\varepsilon$ or of $p$ is required or implied. A model may carry the
additional data of an **equation of state**: a function
$P:D_P\to\mathbb R$ on a subset $D_P\subseteq\mathbb R$ with
$\varepsilon(U)\subseteq D_P$, together with the relation $p=P(\varepsilon)$;
the relation is a further assumption and is not part of the basic triple.

**(b) Stress-energy tensor and derived fields.** The model's
**stress-energy tensor** is

$$T^{ab}:=(\varepsilon+p)n^an^b+p\,g^{ab},$$

a smooth symmetric contravariant $2$-tensor field ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). The **comoving
derivative**, **expansion** and **acceleration** of $n$ are

$$D f:=n^a\partial_af\quad(f\in C^\infty(U)),\qquad \vartheta:=\nabla_an^a,\qquad a^b:=n^a\nabla_an^b ,$$

and the **rest-space projection** is the smooth tensor field

$$h^{ab}:=g^{ab}+n^an^b .$$

The physical reading of $\varepsilon$ and $p$ as a rest-frame energy density
and pressure, and their units, are fixed by the framework's matter postulate,
not by this definition.

**(c) Fluid equations.** The **perfect-fluid equations** on $U$ are

$$D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+p)\vartheta=0,\qquad (\varepsilon+p)a^b+h^{ba}\partial_ap=0 .$$

That the stress-energy tensor is divergence-free if and only if these two
equations hold is proved in
[[prop-gr-dust-and-perfect-fluid-conservation-equations]]; the definition
asserts neither divergence-freedom nor the equations.

This item fixes the unit and coordinate readings of the explicitly defined
Lorentzian objects, smooth-curve proper time and four-velocity of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], the tensor fields of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and the constructed connection,
curvature, Ricci and scalar fields of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]].
It states conventions, not a physical law or a measurement.

**(a) Constants and tensor slot.** Adopt $c>0$ with SI dimension
$\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$, $G_N>0$ with dimension
$\mathrm m^3\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm s^{-2}$, and a signed parameter
$\Lambda$ with dimension $\mathrm m^{-2}$. No numerical value is asserted.
Define $\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$, of dimension
$\mathrm m^{-1}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm s^2$.
For a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $T$ adopt the convention that its
components $T_{AB}=T(e_A,e_B)$ in an ordered $g$-orthonormal basis are energy
per volume, $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$.
This is a tensor slot and unit convention; interpreting a particular $T$ as
matter is a subsequent definition. Therefore $\kappa T_{AB}$ has dimension
$\mathrm m^{-2}$. No positivity, conservation or matter realization is assumed.

**(b) Coordinates and dimensions.** In a length-coordinate chart,
$x^0=ct$ and all four coordinates have units $\mathrm m$; $g_{ab}$ are
dimensionless and the quadratic line element $ds^2=g_{ab}dx^adx^b$ has units
$\mathrm m^2$. The Christoffel symbols defined by
$\nabla^g_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]) have units
$\mathrm m^{-1}$: the constructed formula differentiates dimensionless
$g_{ab}$ once with respect to a length coordinate. Curvature components have
units $\mathrm m^{-2}$ since the curvature operator differentiates the
connection once more and includes products of two connection coefficients;
so do $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$ and scalar curvature $S$ in these coordinates.
In a time-coordinate chart $x^0=t$ has units $\mathrm s$, and $g_{00}$ has
units $\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-2}$; mixed, spatial, angular or other chart
components have the dimensions obtained by the coordinate Jacobians. A single
component has no universal dimension in a general chart. Orthonormal-frame
readings use the normalized geometric basis, with its length normalization.

**(c) Curves and invariant readings.** For the smooth future timelike curve
and positive scaling parameter of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] (e),
read $c$ as in (a) and
$\tau(s)=\tau_0+c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}\,dr$
as a proper-time parameter in seconds. Its four-velocity $U=d\gamma/d\tau$
has length-coordinate and normalized orthonormal components in
$\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$; in a time-coordinate chart $U^0=dt/d\tau$
is dimensionless and other component dimensions follow the coordinates.
Lorentzian length $c\,\Delta\tau$ is in metres. The tensors $R^g$,
$\operatorname{Ric}$ and the scalar $S$ have the orthonormal readings
$\mathrm m^{-2}$, whereas the lowered curvature components in a mixed chart
have the units required by the metric and coordinate slots.

**(d) Future observer readings and SI restoration.** Let $n$ be a future
unit timelike vector, $g(n,n)=-1$ and $g(n,N)<0$. Define
$\rho_n:=T(n,n)$, $j_n:=-\sharp(T(n,\cdot))$ and its spatial part
$\phi_n:=j_n-\rho_n n$; indeed $g(j_n,n)=-\rho_n$, so
$g(\phi_n,n)=0$. In a $g$-orthonormal basis with $e_0=n$, set
$\phi^i=-T(e_0,e_i)=T^{0i}$ for $i=1,2,3$. The **SI energy flux** vector
and **SI momentum density** covector are, respectively,

$$q_n:=c\phi_n,\qquad p_n:=\phi_n^{\flat}/c,\qquad q_n^i=-cT_{0i},\qquad (p_n)_i=-T_{0i}/c.$$

Thus $\rho_n$ and each $\phi^i$ have units $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$;
$q_n^i$ has units $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $(p_n)_i$ has units
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$. Stress components $T_{ij}$ have
units $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{Pa}$. Tensor components retain the
common energy-density units; the factors of $c$ convert their mixed readings
to different SI quantities. Future-directedness and the signs here are part
of the convention, not positivity assumptions on $T$.

**(e) Natural units.** Setting $c=1$, or additionally $G_N=1$, abbreviates
these dimensionful conventions. Restore the factors displayed above before
comparison with SI quantities; in particular the same spatial tensor component
corresponds to energy flux multiplied by $c$ and momentum density divided by
$c$. In a chart whose coordinates $x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3$ are all lengths and whose
metric components are $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, a nonzero null tangent
vector $v=(v^0,\mathbf v)$, null as in clause (b) of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], satisfies
$\|\mathbf v\|_2:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}=|v^0|$. Since $v\ne0$, this
implies $v^0\ne0$, so $\|\mathbf v\|_2/|v^0|=1$. This is a coordinate identity
for the null condition, not a postulate about light propagation, and it does
not change the physical constant $c$.

derivations.claim: (Dust and radiation.) By [L1] the four conditions are read off from the displayed inequalities. For $p=0$ and $\varepsilon>0$: $\varepsilon\ge0$, $\varepsilon+p=\varepsilon>0$, $\varepsilon\ge|p|=0$ and $\varepsilon+3p=\varepsilon>0$, so all four right-hand sides hold. For $p=\varepsilon/3$ and $\varepsilon>0$: $\varepsilon\ge0$, $\varepsilon+p=\tfrac43\varepsilon>0$, $\varepsilon\ge|p|=\varepsilon/3$, and $\varepsilon+3p=2\varepsilon>0$, so all four hold. These are clauses 1 and 2.

(Positive effective fluid.) By [L1] and [L2], let $\varepsilon>0$, $p=-\varepsilon$. Then $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $\varepsilon+p=0\ge0$: WEC holds; $\varepsilon+p=0$: NEC holds; $\varepsilon\ge|p|=\varepsilon$: DEC holds; but $\varepsilon+3p=-2\varepsilon<0$, so SEC fails. This is clause 3.

(Negative effective fluid.) By [L1] and [L2], let $\varepsilon<0$, $p=-\varepsilon>0$. Then $\varepsilon\ge0$ fails, so WEC fails; $\varepsilon\ge|p|=-\varepsilon$ fails (an inequality $t\ge|t|$ with $t<0$ is false), so DEC fails; $\varepsilon+p=0\ge0$, so NEC holds; and $\varepsilon+3p=-2\varepsilon>0$ together with $\varepsilon+p=0$ gives SEC. This is clause 4 and shows that SEC need not imply WEC or DEC. Clause 3 shows that WEC need not imply SEC, so WEC and SEC are incomparable. These examples are consistent with the implications DEC $\Rightarrow$ WEC $\Rightarrow$ NEC and SEC $\Rightarrow$ NEC proved in [[def-gr-energy-conditions]].

boundaries.reason: The verdicts are algebraic statements about prescribed values of energy density and pressure; no empty-dataset or empty-domain case arises.

boundaries.evidence: clauses 3 and 4: the vanishing of energy density plus pressure is the equality case of the null and weak conditions and is exactly the value tested in steps 1.2 and 2.1.
step 1.1: the single substitution of one third of the energy density decides all four conditions for radiation, with the strong combination equal to twice the density.
steps 1.2 and 2.1 treat the vanishing of energy density plus pressure, the degenerate case of the acceleration equation, where the null condition holds with equality.

boundaries.reason: The strict-timelike convention of the cited equivalences leaves the cone boundary untested, so no boundary inequality is asserted.
Each clause is a direct substitution into the displayed equivalences; nothing is selected.

boundaries.evidence: steps 1.1-2.1 read each equivalence in the direction condition implies displayed inequalities.
steps 1.1-2.1 read each equivalence in the direction displayed inequalities imply condition, which is how the failing verdicts are certified.

risk_review.notes: Read all three steps and exact rest-frame equivalences. Substitution gives all four conditions for positive dust/radiation; positive effective fluid p=-epsilon gives WEC/NEC/DEC and fails SEC; negative effective fluid fails WEC/DEC but satisfies NEC/SEC. Thus WEC and SEC are incomparable by explicit witnesses. Kappa>0 gives epsilon=Lambda/kappa and p=-Lambda/kappa; the comparison is pointwise and asserts no solution or nature claim. Equality cases and zero causal current are covered by the earlier definitions; DEC=>WEC=>NEC and SEC=>NEC are actually proved in the energy-condition definition.

The note records conventions and obligations rather than equations, so there is no vanishing parameter to dispose of.
No dimension or size parameter occurs in the note, so the single-object axis has no referent.
